findings.title: The iOS test target will likely fail to compile on its first run (deployment target 13.0 vs 14.0, no pod search paths)
findings.why_it_matters: `PlayerTimeUtilsTests` does `@testable import Audiobookshelf`. The test target is set to iOS 13.0, while the app target and every pod are built for 14.0 (`platform :ios, '14.0'`). Swift refuses to import a module built for a higher minimum deployment target. Separately, the test target has no Pods search paths, and the app's swiftmodule imports RealmSwift and Alamofire, so "missing required module 'RealmSwift'" is the classic failure for app-hosted tests without the nested Podfile target. The ledger treats the Podfile block as a maybe and plans to discover it. Discovering it costs a failed ~25-minute macOS run. A Podfile change also changes `Podfile.lock`'s checksum, so `pod install --deployment` fails until the lock is regenerated through `refresh-pod-lock.yml` and committed back. Each discovery is a multi-step round trip on a PR that can only merge green.
findings.recommended: A: Align the test target's deployment target to 14.0 and add the nested `target 'AudiobookshelfUnitTests' do inherit! :search_paths end` in the first commit, regenerating `Podfile.lock` before the first iOS run
findings.chosen: A: Align the test target's deployment target to 14.0 and add the nested `target 'AudiobookshelfUnitTests' do inherit! :search_paths end` in the first commit, regenerating `Podfile.lock` before the first iOS run

findings.title: Copying the repo's `npm ci --omit=optional` into `js-tests` breaks Vitest
findings.why_it_matters: Vite's bundler (rollup) and esbuild ship their platform binaries as optionalDependencies. Every existing job installs with `npm ci --omit=optional`. A `js-tests` job written by copying that step fails with "Cannot find module @rollup/rollup-linux-x64-gnu" (or the esbuild equivalent), and the error doesn't point back at the install flag. The flag exists to skip fsevents 1.x and its native-build dependencies (added in bf92d18b, when the lock carried `fsevents`/`nan`/`bindings`). The only optional packages with install scripts in today's lock are the two `fsevents` copies, both `"os": ["darwin"]`, which npm skips on ubuntu anyway. So plain `npm ci` loses nothing in an ubuntu job. The other jobs keep the flag safely because they never run Vitest.
findings.recommended: A: Install with plain `npm ci` in `js-tests`, with a comment that the other jobs' `--omit=optional` exists for darwin-only fsevents
findings.chosen: A: Install with plain `npm ci` in `js-tests`, with a comment that the other jobs' `--omit=optional` exists for darwin-only fsevents

findings.title: D4 never says which simulator `test-without-building` runs on, and a hard-coded name breaks on runner-image updates
findings.why_it_matters: D4 says the build step's "action and destination change" and that tests run "against a concrete simulator", but it never says which one or how it's chosen. The usual shortcut is `-destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 16'`. That breaks with "Unable to find a destination" whenever GitHub changes the simulator set on `macos-15-intel`, an unpinned label on a deprecation path. The result is a red PR caused by a runner-image change, not by the product. The two steps must also share `-derivedDataPath build`, `-scheme`, `-configuration`, `-sdk` and the `ASSETCATALOG_COMPILER_APPICON_NAME`/`CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED` overrides. Otherwise `test-without-building` can't find the `.xctestrun` or tests a mismatched build. The ledger specifies none of this.
findings.recommended: A: Resolve an available iPhone simulator's UDID once, log it, and pass `-destination "id=$UDID"` plus the same derived-data path and build settings to both `build-for-testing` and `test-without-building`
findings.chosen: A: Resolve an available iPhone simulator's UDID once, log it, and pass `-destination "id=$UDID"` plus the same derived-data path and build settings to both `build-for-testing` and `test-without-building`

findings.title: A green job is taken as proof the tests ran, and only a human-read summary catches a test that silently dropped out
findings.why_it_matters: `ci-complete` treats each job's `success` as proof the harness works. The ledger itself says "a test missing from the target passes silently, so the step summary is the check". That check is a page someone has to open and read. In the hand-registered iOS project, an upstream merge that touches `project.pbxproj` or the scheme can drop `PlayerTimeUtilsTests` from the Sources phase or the scheme's testables. The job then runs zero tests and goes green. Android's `testDebugUnitTest` on Gradle 8.11 also passes when no tests are found. Vitest is the exception: by default it exits 1 when no test files are found, as long as `passWithNoTests` stays off.
findings.recommended: B: Fail the iOS test step unless `PlayerTimeUtilsTests` executed; rely on Vitest's default and the Android job result elsewhere
findings.chosen: B: Fail the iOS test step unless `PlayerTimeUtilsTests` executed; rely on Vitest's default and the Android job result elsewhere

findings.title: The iOS test step has no stated timeout or job budget, and a hang or crashed app host leaves little to diagnose
findings.why_it_matters: The tests are app-hosted, so `test-without-building` boots a simulator and launches the full app (Capacitor WebView, Realm) before injecting the bundle. Host crashes, slow or wedged simulator boots, and runner-connection timeouts are the classic hang modes. The Posture says a hang "fails at the test step's own timeout", but the ledger gives no value. The job's `timeout-minutes: 45` is shared with a ~25-minute build. If the step timeout is too large, the job timeout fires first, and an upload gated on `if: failure()` doesn't run on a cancelled job. If it's too small, it kills a legitimately slow cold boot. The `.xcresult` is the only artifact planned. When the app host crashes at launch, it reads "failed to bootstrap" and carries no crash log.
findings.recommended: A: Give the test step a stated timeout (about 12-15 min), set the job timeout above build time plus that, and upload the `.xcresult` whenever the step doesn't succeed, including on cancel
findings.chosen: A: Give the test step a stated timeout (about 12-15 min), set the job timeout above build time plus that, and upload the `.xcresult` whenever the step doesn't succeed, including on cancel

findings.title: D5 expects the wrong failure: the test's expectations are correct, and the hidden dependency is Realm state, not the clock
findings.why_it_matters: D5's Situation predicts the test may fail on clock timing or stale expectations. The assertions match the current thresholds (<10s → 0, <60 → 3, <300 → 10, <1800 → 20, else 30). The clock offsets (2, 12, 62, 302, 1802s) sit well inside their buckets, so a runner stall of a few seconds won't flip them. The dependency D5 misses is `isAutoRewindDisabled()`, which reads `Database.shared.getDeviceSettings()`, Realm inside the app-hosted process. It defaults to `false`, so a clean simulator passes. A Realm init failure or persisted setting in the host turns into a wrong value on every case or a crashed test process. That failure is neither "the test's fault" nor "the code's fault" as D5 frames them. The test's inline comments ("should seek back 5s", "15s") also disagree with its assertions. A reader may take the comments as evidence of stale expectations when the assertions are right.
findings.chosen: Rewrite D5's Situation: the assertions match `PlayerTimeUtils`' current thresholds and the clock offsets sit well inside their buckets, so timing is a low risk. The real hidden dependency is `isAutoRewindDisabled()` reading `Database.shared.getDeviceSettings()` (Realm, in the app host; default `false`). The test's inline comments are stale, not its assertions. In the Recommendation's "test's fault" branch, add that pinning `disableAutoRewind` in the test's `setUp` is a permitted test fix.

findings.title: `build-for-testing` keeps `-quiet`, so a test-target compile error fails the build step with no useful log
findings.why_it_matters: D4 ratified that a broken test target now fails the build step. The ledger drops `-quiet` only from the test step. The build step still runs `xcodebuild -quiet`, so a test-target compile or link failure, the likely first-run outcome per Finding 1, reports in the same terse way as an app compile error. Both critics ask for `-quiet` off in `build-for-testing` as well. Renaming the step is also safe if wanted: `ci-complete` keys off the job id `ios` through `needs`, not the step or job display name, and branch protection is on `ci-complete` alone.
findings.chosen: In D4, state that `build-for-testing` also runs without `-quiet`, so the step that fails on a broken test target shows which target failed and why.

findings.title: The `js-tests` path filter is unspecified, and the ledger's `ci-complete` bullet lists three of six touch points
findings.why_it_matters: The Summary says `js-tests` gets "its own path filter" but doesn't give one. It also says the job needs three `ci-complete` edits ("Without all three, a red JS job wouldn't block the merge"). Wiring the job actually takes six: a `changes` output, a `paths-filter` entry, the job's `if:`, plus the `needs` entry, env pair and `check` call. The `if:` and the `*_WANTED` expression are hand-copied twins. If they diverge, a job that runs when "not wanted" fails `ci-complete`. A filter that misses a test-relevant path leaves `js-tests` skipped, and `ci-complete` reads that skip as a pass. Separately, the `android` and `ios` filters are `'**'` minus exclusions, so a PR touching only `test/**` starts the ~25-minute macOS build. That cuts against D4's deciding factor, which is macOS minutes.
findings.recommended: A: List all six touch points in the `ci-complete` bullet, give `js-tests` a `'**'`-minus filter (`ios/**`, `android/**`, `**/*.md`, `design/**`), and add `!test/**` to the `android` and `ios` filters
findings.chosen: A: List all six touch points in the `ci-complete` bullet, give `js-tests` a `'**'`-minus filter (`ios/**`, `android/**`, `**/*.md`, `design/**`), and add `!test/**` to the `android` and `ios` filters

findings.title: Android runs Gradle twice (tests, then `assembleDebug`), each paying a cold `--no-daemon` start
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger runs the JVM tests as their own step before the keystore install and `assembleDebug`. With `--no-daemon`, each invocation pays JVM startup and Gradle configuration, roughly 1-2 minutes extra on the ubuntu runner. Both critics propose one invocation, `./android/gradlew testDebugUnitTest assembleDebug`. One critic's claim that Kotlin and kapt compile twice overstates it: Gradle's up-to-date checks persist on disk across invocations, so `assembleDebug` reuses the compiled classes, and the cost is startup and configuration only. The single invocation has to sit after the keystore step, because the debug signing config attaches only when the keystore exists. Merging the two also gives up the ledger's "own step" for tests, which says at a glance whether a test or the APK build failed.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the tests as their own step before the keystore install, accepting the extra Gradle start
findings.chosen: B: Keep the tests as their own step before the keystore install, accepting the extra Gradle start

findings.title: The Android test's "pure function" must have no `android.*` calls, or the JVM test throws "Method not mocked"
findings.why_it_matters: The Summary picks "an existing pure function" for the Kotlin JVM test. Plain JVM unit tests run against the stub `android.jar`, and `testOptions.unitTests.returnDefaultValues` is not set. So any function that touches `android.util.Log`, `Build`, or similar throws "Method ... not mocked" at runtime, even if it is pure in the logical sense. The parent ledger rules out framework stubbing (no Robolectric), so the function has to avoid the framework entirely.
findings.chosen: In the Summary's Android bullet, change "an existing pure function" to "an existing pure function with no `android.*` calls (JVM unit tests run against the stub `android.jar`; `returnDefaultValues` is not set)".

findings.title: D3's component smoke test needs `vue-template-compiler` pinned to the Vue version
Findings converge on D8's silent-drop-out guard (one named iOS canary)
findings.why_it_matters: D8 ("Does CI fail when a test silently stops running?") settled on one mechanism: on iOS only, require that a test in one named class, `PlayerTimeUtilsTests`, passed. JS was judged safe because Vitest fails on zero test files, and Android was left unguarded "until real Android tests arrive". Three findings from two critics hit that mechanism from different sides. The Vitest `include` glob can drop new tests without zero files ever being reached (Finding 3). The iOS canary covers one class while #8/#9 are about to add the tests that matter (Finding 4). Android's exemption was conditioned on real tests not existing, and this change adds three (Finding 5). Each has its own local patch: widen a glob, extend a name list, add an XML count. Applied separately, they grow three unrelated per-side checks on top of a premise that has already gone stale. The question for you is whether D8's model of "tests silently stopped running" should be re-decided as a whole, including whether accepting and documenting the gap per side is the right answer, rather than patched finding by finding.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate D8's silent-drop-out guard before addressing Findings 3, 4 and 5 individually. Open questions: Does each side need a guard at all, given peers carry none? Should JS's "fails on zero files" still count as a guard when a wrong filename gets no signal? Is the trigger for revisiting Android ("real tests arrive") now met? Should the iOS guard follow #8/#9's tests or stay a harness smoke check? Which of these is a known limitation to record in D8 instead of a check?
findings.chosen: Other: re-decided D8 as a whole: convention-based discovery on every side, zero-tests check on iOS, synchronized test folder (D11)
findings.choice_reason: User: simplify to convention-based test discovery and ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: The final iOS commit (SDK-capped picker) has no completed run, so both its correctness and the 15-minute test-step budget are unverified
findings.why_it_matters: D9 ratified a 15-minute test-step timeout, sized only against the job budget, before any test step had run. The only measured test step took 13.4 of its 15 minutes, on run 43507734347, which booted an iOS 26.2 simulator under Xcode 16.4. The Build section attributes about 10.5 of those minutes to that runtime and added the SDK-capped picker in 853a01af to avoid it. That attribution is an inference: the run log doesn't separate runtime provisioning from a cold simulator boot on the Intel runner, and boot and host launch happen inside one opaque `xcodebuild` step. If cold boot was the cause, the picker changes nothing and the headroom stays near 1.6 minutes. Separately, the green run that is cited predates the picker, so nothing yet ties a passing iOS run to the commit being shipped. With no retries (Posture), a slow but healthy boot that crosses 15 minutes reads as a hang, fails `ci-complete`, and has to be re-run by hand on a scarce macOS runner.
findings.recommended: A: Wait for the in-progress re-run. Record the test step's duration in Build. Keep 15 if the step finishes with a wide margin (roughly 8 minutes or less), otherwise raise the step to 20. The job's 55 covers either.
findings.chosen: A: Wait for the in-progress re-run. Record the test step's duration in Build. Keep 15 if the step finishes with a wide margin (roughly 8 minutes or less), otherwise raise the step to 20. The job's 55 covers either.

findings.title: Vitest's hand-written `include` glob is narrower than the default, so a later test with another name or extension never runs and the job stays green
findings.why_it_matters: D8 counted JS as guarded because Vitest exits 1 when it finds no test files. That only fires at zero. `vitest.config.mjs` narrows collection to `test/js/**/*.test.js`, while Vitest's own default is `**/*.{test,spec}.?(c|m)[jt]s?(x)`. A later test named `*.spec.js`, `*.test.mjs` or `*.test.ts` is never collected. The two existing files still match, so `npm test` passes and `js-tests` reports success. That is the same "a test silently stops running" failure D8 set out to prevent, in a place its guard can't see. Nothing in the tree depends on the narrower pattern: `test/` contains only `test/js/`.
findings.recommended: A: Replace `include: ['test/js/**/*.test.js']` with `dir: 'test/js'` so Vitest's default test pattern applies under `test/js/`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The iOS canary proves one test class survived, and #8/#9 are about to add the XCTests that matter
findings.why_it_matters: D8 put the iOS guard where it did because the project registers files by hand, and an upstream merge touching `project.pbxproj` can drop tests from the target. The check requires only that some `PlayerTimeUtilsTests/...` case passed. The contract and sleep-timer XCTests that #8/#9 add to the same target would be dropped by exactly that merge, and the canary would stay green as long as `PlayerTimeUtilsTests` survives. Today the canary covers everything that exists, so this is a stance question about #8/#9 and not a defect in the code.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the canary as is, and add to D8's Ratified sentence that #8/#9 must extend the check to the tests they add.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Android has no tests-ran guard, and D8's stated condition for that ("until real Android tests arrive") is already met
findings.why_it_matters: D8 accepted that "an Android source-set misconfiguration still passes green until real Android tests arrive". This change adds three real Android tests (`AudioTrackTest.kt`), so the accepted clause now describes a condition that has passed. The silent path is narrow. If an upstream merge deletes or moves `android/app/src/test`, Gradle reports NO-SOURCE and succeeds. A lost `testImplementation` line fails compilation loudly, so that path is not silent. A guard is cheap: count `<testcase` elements in `android/app/build/test-results/testDebugUnitTest/*.xml`.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: Android's test step passes green if its test sources disappear in a merge; reword D8's accepting clause from "until real Android tests arrive" to name that limitation and the #8/#9 revisit.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: The `.xcresult` upload fires on any earlier step's failure, wider than D9's "whenever the step doesn't succeed"
findings.why_it_matters: D9 ratified uploading the `.xcresult` "whenever the step doesn't succeed (including on cancel)". The code gates the upload on job-level `failure() || cancelled()`. So a failed `pod install` or `build-for-testing` also runs the upload. No bundle exists then, and `if-no-files-found: warn` adds a "no files found" warning to the failed run, on a step unrelated to where the failure was. It is harmless but misleading. The Build section doesn't record the difference, so the code and the ratified wording disagree on every read. Senior-engineer's proposed `steps.<id>.outcome == 'failure'` would also drop the cancel case, which D9 explicitly wants. Contract-caller's form keeps it.
findings.recommended: A: Give "Run iOS unit tests" an `id` (e.g. `tests`) and set the upload's `if:` to `(failure() || cancelled()) && steps.tests.conclusion != 'skipped'`.
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: simplify to convention-based test discovery and ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: The `ios` job's timeout comment states a build duration the observed run contradicts
findings.why_it_matters: The comment above `timeout-minutes: 55` says "The build takes about 25 minutes; this leaves room for the test step's own 15-minute timeout plus the install and pod steps". The 25-minute figure was the whole old job (D4 Situation: "about 25 minutes of job time"; D9: "~24.5 minutes"), not the build step. It already includes the install and pod steps the comment adds on top. On the observed run, `build-for-testing` took about 8.3 minutes and the whole job 27. Anyone resizing these timeouts later (Findings 2 and 8) starts from a wrong figure. Because the problem is in the comment, it exists on every read.
findings.chosen: Replace the two comment lines at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:135-136` with a single numberless line stating the invariant: `# Leaves room for the setup, build and test steps' own timeouts, so a hung test fails at its step and still uploads results.` Leave `timeout-minutes` unchanged. Findings 2 and 8 decide the numbers.

findings.title: Raising the `ios` job to 55 minutes lengthens how long a wedged pre-test step can hold the runner
findings.why_it_matters: D9 raised the job from 45 to 55 on the assumption that a ~25-minute build plus a 15-minute test step left under 5 minutes of headroom at 45. The observed run puts everything except the test step at about 13.6 minutes (27 total minus 13.4), so even a test step that runs to its 15-minute timeout ends near 29 minutes, well inside 45. The extra 10 minutes therefore buy nothing for the test-step hang D9 was about. They do let the steps with no timeout of their own (`pod install`, the picker's `simctl`, `build-for-testing`) hold a scarce Intel macOS runner 10 minutes longer if one wedges. This rests on the run facts, which the in-progress re-run will refresh. If Finding 2 raises the step to 20-25, 45 still covers it on these numbers.
findings.recommended: C: Accept as a known limitation: a wedged pod, picker or build step can hold the macOS runner up to 55 minutes instead of 45.
findings.chosen: A: Revert the `ios` job to `timeout-minutes: 45` and update D9's Ratified numbers.

findings.title: `js-tests` runs on Node 24 while the Android job builds the web app on Node 20
findings.why_it_matters: The `android` job runs `npm run generate` on Node 20, and `js-tests` runs on Node 24. In principle, a test could pass on 24 while the tested code behaves differently under the Android build's Node. The `ios` job also generates on Node 24, so the web layer is already built on both versions, and `js-tests` matches one of them. The current tests exercise `store/` getters and a leaf component, so a Node-version-only difference is improbable.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `js-tests` runs on Node 24, matching the iOS build but not the Android build's Node 20.
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: The Android job installs Vite 7 on Node 20, whose `engines` needs 20.19 or later
findings.why_it_matters: The `android` job's `npm ci --omit=optional` now installs the new devDependencies, including `vite` 7.3.8 with `engines.node` `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0`. `npm ci` only warns on an engines mismatch unless `engine-strict` is set, the repo has no `.npmrc`, and `setup-node` with `20` resolves to the newest 20.x, which is above 20.19. The Android job never runs Vite or Vitest; it only installs them. It would break only if `engine-strict` were turned on or the toolchain were pinned to an older 20.x. The critic's suggested `--ignore-scripts` would not change this, because the engines check isn't an install script.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the Android job installs Vite 7 on Node 20 with at most an engines warning; it would fail only under `engine-strict` or a Node pinned below 20.19.
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: The simulator picker's device choice within a runtime depends on `simctl`'s listing order
findings.why_it_matters: `sort_by(.version) | last` ties every iPhone on the newest qualifying runtime, so the winner is the last-listed one. jq's sort is stable, so for a given runner image the same device is picked each time; my mock-input run gave the same pick on every call. The device changes when the image's simulator set or ordering changes, and boot time differs by model, which adds noise when comparing run timings (Finding 2). Unit tests don't depend on the model, so correctness is unaffected, and the chosen name is already logged. The proposed `sort_by([.version, .name])` would pick by lexicographic name instead, which favors e.g. "iPhone SE (3rd generation)" over "iPhone 16", since `S` sorts after `1`. That is still image-dependent whenever the device set changes.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: the simulator is the last-listed iPhone on the chosen runtime, stable per runner image, and logged as "Using simulator".
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: The picker's version comparison mishandles an SDK version printed without a minor component
findings.why_it_matters: jq compares arrays element by element, and a shorter array sorts first: `[26,0] <= [26]` is `false` (checked: `jq -n '[26,0] <= [26]'` prints `false`). If `xcrun --show-sdk-version` ever printed a bare `26`, runtime iOS 26.0 would be excluded. In the mock run with SDK `26`, the picker fell back to the iOS 18.5 runtime. With no older runtime it fails loudly via `::error::No available iPhone simulator`. Either way nothing passes silently. No critic confirmed that any Xcode prints a bare major version.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a simulator SDK version printed as a bare major (e.g. `26`) makes the picker skip that major's `.0` runtime, falling back to an older one or failing with "No available iPhone simulator".
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: ignore the critics' edge cases

findings.title: A future JS test that reads native sources would be skipped on native-only PRs, and `ci-complete` reads the skip as a pass
findings.why_it_matters: The `js` filter excludes `ios/**` and `android/**` (D10), which is right for tests of isolated JS modules. If someone later puts a test under `test/js/` that reads native files (a parity-style check), a PR touching only native code would skip `js-tests`, and `ci-complete` treats a skipped, unwanted job as success. The parent ledger already plans the parity check as its own job with its own filter, and keeps #8's contract fixture outside the excluded paths, so #7 and #8 as planned are safe. The gap opens only if a native-reading check ends up in `test/js/`.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `js-tests` doesn't run on native-only PRs, so a JS test that reads native files would pass by skip; record it in D10's accepting clause.
findings.chosen: Skip — defer to later
findings.choice_reason: User: ignore the critics' edge cases
